issues.subcategory: participant flow arithmetic mismatch
issues.description: The reported participant flow does not add up. The manuscript reports 468 respondents at Time 1 and 450 at Time 4, implying 18 participants did not complete all waves, but later says only 16 were excluded for missing time points. Also, 468 minus 16 missing-time exclusions minus 78 data-quality exclusions equals 374, not the stated final N of 372. If the exclusions are from the 450 completers, then the missing-time exclusion should be 18. This undermines confidence in the analytic sample definition and reproducibility of the analyses.
issues.quote: n = 468 nurses responded at time 1; n = 458 responded at time 2 (98% retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 (98% retention rate between T2 and T3); and n = 450 responded at time 4 (98% retention rate between T3 and T4). ... Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample. ... This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: incorrect retention-rate calculations
issues.description: The stated 98% retention rates are inaccurate for later waves. T3 retention from T2 is 454/458 = 99.1%, and T4 retention from T3 is 450/454 = 99.1%, not 98%. While small, this is a basic reporting/calculation error in the participant flow.
issues.quote: n = 458 responded at time 2 (98% retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 (98% retention rate between T2 and T3); and n = 450 responded at time 4 (98% retention rate between T3 and T4).

issues.subcategory: unexplained analytic sample-size discrepancies
issues.description: The final sample is reported as N = 372, but the main descriptive and mediation tables use N = 321, and the moderation table uses N = 244. The reduction from 372 to 321 is not explained, and the reduction to 244 is only attributed generally to moderator missingness. These unexplained discrepancies make it unclear which observations contributed to each analysis and whether missing data were handled consistently.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372. ... Note. N = 321. Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal. ... Note. N = 321. * p < .05 ** p < .01 *** p < .001 ... Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.subcategory: complete-case analysis after forced monotone attrition
issues.description: Participants who missed one wave were not invited to subsequent waves, creating design-induced monotone attrition. The analysis then included only complete cases. This can bias longitudinal estimates if missingness is related to workload, stress, incivility, fatigue, or shift scheduling. The comparison described only T1-only respondents and used a vague 'within one standard deviation' criterion rather than formal attrition modeling or modern missing-data methods.
issues.quote: Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys). ... Only participants who completed all four surveys ... were included in the final sample. ... Participants who responded only to the T1 survey reported similar demographic information compared to those who completed all four time periods and had scale values on the key study constructs within one standard deviation of the means for the final sample

issues.subcategory: large missingness on moderator handled inadequately
issues.description: Perceived patient acuity had substantial missingness: the moderation model used N = 244 versus a final sample of 372, implying about one-third of participants were excluded. The manuscript does not report the exact missing count in the text, does not use FIML or multiple imputation, and only compares demographics/workplace characteristics rather than key study constructs or missingness mechanisms. Listwise deletion can bias moderation and moderated mediation estimates and reduces power.
issues.quote: Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response). However, a comparison of personal demographics and workplace characteristics did not find any significant differences between participants with and without missing values for perceived patient acuity. ... Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.subcategory: patient acuity operationalized with an unvalidated single subjective item
issues.description: Patient acuity is a clinical/workload construct, but it was measured by a single self-reported estimate of the percentage of patients considered 'severe' across heterogeneous units and acuity systems. This conflates actual acuity, perceived workload, respondent affect, recall, number of patients seen, and local scale differences. Because patient acuity is central to the moderation hypothesis, weak operationalization threatens construct validity and interpretation of the interaction.
issues.quote: we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.” ... “Based on your department's patient acuity scale ... what percentage of patients under your care in the past week would be considered "severe"?”

issues.subcategory: main-study missing/out-of-range acuity responses contradict pilot validity claims
issues.description: The pilot reportedly showed that all nurses understood and could answer the patient acuity item, yet in the main study a large fraction of acuity data were missing or outside the expected numerical range. This suggests the item was not actually clear or standardized enough for the target population, undermining the validity of the moderator.
issues.quote: For the quantitative pilot, all participants provided an answer to the perceived patient acuity question, responded that they felt capable of accurately responding to the item, and that it was applicable to their patients. ... For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).

issues.subcategory: ambiguous percentage-response coding for patient acuity
issues.description: The acuity item asks for a percentage, but the table reports means around .52-.54, implying proportions rather than 0-100 percentages. The manuscript does not specify the response format, whether entries such as '75' versus '.75' were accepted or converted, or what counted as outside the expected range. Given that 45% of acuity missingness came from out-of-range responses, this omission is consequential for replication and validity.
issues.quote: what percentage of patients under your care in the past week would be considered "severe"? ... T1 Patient Acuity | .54 | .25 ... T2 Patient Acuity | .52 | .28 ... the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).

issues.subcategory: nonprobability self-selected convenience sample
issues.description: Participants were recruited through flyers, personal networks, social media, forums, and a hospital news forum, with an unknown sampling frame and no response rate. This creates strong self-selection risk, especially for a study about work experiences, wellbeing, and incivility. The resulting sample cannot be treated as representative of nurses, critical-care nurses, or service workers generally.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies. First, we dropped off recruitment flyers ... Second, we sent emails to nurses and other healthcare professionals in our personal networks ... Finally, we posted study information and recruitment materials online via personal social network accounts ... Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown

issues.subcategory: eligibility and duplicate participation not adequately controlled
issues.description: Recruitment used public links/QR codes and participant-initiated enrollment, with no clear verification of nursing licensure, employment, unit, or uniqueness. The fact that 21 responses were excluded for duplicate/collusive open-ended responses indicates a real data-integrity problem. Reliance on post hoc exclusions rather than unique invitations or credential verification weakens confidence in sample validity.
issues.quote: participants initiated the contact and study procedures by clicking on the study link or QR code that was listed in recruitment materials ... duplicate responses (identical content, syntax, and formatting) to open ended attention check questions as other participants (suggesting repeat survey participation and/or collusion) (n = 21).

issues.subcategory: inclusion criteria conflict: full-time versus part-time nurses
issues.description: The recruitment materials stated that inclusion required working full time in high-stakes/critical care as a nurse, but the final sample description says participants could be part- or full-time. This inconsistency changes the target population and may affect exposure, workload, and weekly recall periods.
issues.quote: Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse) ... All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time), worked more than one shift a week, on average, and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients.

issues.subcategory: no accounting for hospital/unit nesting
issues.description: Nurses were recruited from multiple hospitals and likely nested within hospitals, units, specialties, and recruitment networks. Unit culture, staffing ratios, management practices, patient populations, and local incivility climates could affect both experienced and enacted incivility. The analyses do not report multilevel modeling, cluster-robust standard errors, fixed effects, or even hospital/unit identifiers, so standard errors and substantive conclusions may be biased.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. ... A healthcare sample was specifically selected ... nurses working with multiple patients simultaneously and transferring care to other nurses at the end of their shifts.

issues.subcategory: single-source self-report for predictor, mediators, moderator, and outcome
issues.description: All focal variables, including socially undesirable enacted incivility, were self-reported by the same respondent. This raises common-method, negative-affectivity, recall, consistency-motif, and social-desirability concerns. Temporal separation helps only partially and does not address the same-source measurement of enacted mistreatment toward patients.
issues.quote: This study is a four-wave panel longitudinal design that will include administration of self-report online questionnaires ... Enacted Incivility. Four items ... were used to measure the frequency participants instigated incivility towards their patients. Participants were asked, “Thinking about your interactions with patients during the past week, how often have you…?”

issues.subcategory: claim of temporal separation contradicted by same-wave mediator and outcome
issues.description: The manuscript claims that each measure in the hypothesized model was temporally separated, but compassion fatigue and enacted incivility are both measured at Time 4. This directly contradicts the claimed design advantage and weakens the serial mediation inference.
issues.quote: our multiwave approach allows for temporal separation of each measure in our hypothesized model ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... T4 Enacted Incivility

issues.subcategory: serial mediation lacks temporal ordering for final path
issues.description: Hypothesis 4 requires compassion fatigue to precede enacted incivility, but both are assessed in the same Time 4 survey with the same past-week recall period. The final mediator-outcome association is therefore contemporaneous, not longitudinal, and cannot establish that compassion fatigue predicts later enacted incivility.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 4 predicted that experienced patient incivility would be positively indirectly related to enacted incivility toward patients through negative emotions toward patients and compassion fatigue. ... Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... T4 Enacted Incivility

issues.subcategory: causal language from observational panel data
issues.description: The study is observational, nonrandomized, and entirely self-report, yet repeatedly uses causal language such as 'leads to,' 'impacts,' and 'causal inferences.' Autoregressive controls and temporal ordering reduce some ambiguity but do not rule out confounding, reverse causation, stable response tendencies, unit-level factors, or omitted variables. Causal claims should be substantially softened.
issues.quote: This method also supports a lower likelihood of third variable effects ... and allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time. ... These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.subcategory: reverse causality not modeled
issues.description: The theoretical title and model assume experienced incivility begets enacted incivility, but enacted incivility toward patients could also provoke patient or family incivility, and prior burnout/negative affect could increase perceived incivility. The analysis does not report alternative cross-lagged or reciprocal models despite measuring all constructs at each wave.
issues.quote: To better understand the effect of the predictor variables on the criterion variable at the subsequent time point, we assessed each variable during each wave. ... Incivility begets incivility

issues.subcategory: selective use of waves and unspecified model-selection rationale
issues.description: Although each variable was measured at all four waves, the focal model uses T2 experienced incivility, T3 negative emotions, and T4 compassion fatigue/enacted incivility, with T1 reserved as baseline. The manuscript does not report preregistration, alternative lag specifications, stationarity tests, or sensitivity analyses using other adjacent waves. This creates substantial researcher degrees of freedom in longitudinal model specification.
issues.quote: we assessed each variable during each wave. ... Because it was impossible to account for same or other variable effects prior to the first time point in our study, the first wave was reserved for controlling for autoregressive effects, and the subsequent waves were included for hypothesis testing

issues.subcategory: autoregressive controls and within-wave covariances not fully reported
issues.description: The analytic strategy states that AR(1) paths and covariances among all variables within each wave were modeled, but the tables do not show the baseline autoregressive paths, same-wave covariances, or full control-variable estimates. Without the full model specification and estimates, readers cannot evaluate whether the reported coefficients are truly adjusted as described.
issues.quote: This allowed us to assess stability over time by modeling the autocorrelations (AR1) between each variable and its prior occasions and the covariances between all variables (including controls) within each wave ... Table 2 ... Variables | ... T2 Customer Incivility ... T3 Negative Emotions ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... T2 Work Hours ... T3 Work Hours

issues.subcategory: CFA model-comparison reporting appears malformed and insufficient
issues.description: The CFA paragraph reports fit statistics in a way that is statistically unclear: chi-square symbols are missing, comparison models are reported with implausibly tiny degrees of freedom for item-level CFA, and it is unclear whether the reported values are model chi-squares or difference tests. With WLSMV estimation, chi-square difference testing requires special procedures. The reporting is not adequate to verify the claimed superior four-factor model.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than a three-factor model wherein both incivility measures were set to load onto the same factor (3) = 82.52, RMSEA = .09, CFI = .98, TLI = .98), a two-factor model ... (2) = 82.65, RMSEA = .10, CFI = .98, TLI = .98), and a one-factor model (1) = 8.02, RMSEA = .10, CFI = .98, TLI = .98).

issues.subcategory: poor discriminant validity among focal constructs
issues.description: Several focal constructs are correlated extremely highly, including negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility. Correlations around .90-.96 suggest empirical redundancy, shared method variance, or construct overlap. This undermines claims that the mediators and outcome are distinct mechanisms and raises concern that the serial mediation is partly an artifact of non-discriminant measures.
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .85 | .86 | .96 ... T4 Enacted Incivility ... .82 | .87 | .94 | .91

issues.subcategory: multicollinearity threatens regression and mediation estimates
issues.description: The very high correlations among predictors in the final regression, especially negative emotions and compassion fatigue, imply severe multicollinearity. This can make path coefficients unstable, produce suppression effects, and distort interpretations of relative importance and indirect effects. The manuscript does not report VIFs, condition indices, or sensitivity analyses.
issues.quote: T3 Negative Emotions ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .96 ... T4 Enacted Incivility ... .94 | .91

issues.subcategory: indirect-effect arithmetic inconsistency
issues.description: The reported H2 indirect effect does not match the product of the reported constituent paths. The text gives path a = .26 and path d = .37, whose product is .096, not .07. This could reflect rounding, different models, or omitted controls, but the discrepancy is large enough to require clarification.
issues.quote: experienced patient incivility was positively related to negative emotions toward patients (B = .26, SE = .06, p < .001). ... Time 3 negative emotions toward patients were positively related to Time 4 compassion fatigue (B = .37, SE = .04, p < .001). ... the positive indirect relationship ... was significant (B = .07, SE = .03, p < .05, 95% CI [0.02, 0.14]).

issues.subcategory: inconsistent SE, p-value, and confidence interval for H4 indirect effect
issues.description: For the H4 indirect effect, the text reports B = .06 with SE = .04 and p < .01, but B/SE = 1.5 would not yield p < .01, and the 95% CI [0.02, 0.10] implies an SE closer to .02. Table 2 also reports SE = .02. This is an internal statistical reporting error affecting a central hypothesis.
issues.quote: Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]). ... Customer Incivility  Negative Emotions  Compassion Fatigue  Enacted Incivility | .06** | .02 | 2.58

issues.subcategory: supplemental regression coefficients conflict with main model
issues.description: The supplemental relative-importance regression reports coefficients that differ substantially from the main mediation table. For example, compassion fatigue predicts enacted incivility at B = .57 in Table 2 but B = .23 in the supplemental regression. The text also says the compassion fatigue estimate is nearly six times negative emotions, but Table 2 shows .57 versus .28, about two times. These inconsistencies make the supplemental interpretation unreliable.
issues.quote: the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue that is nearly six times that of negative emotions. ... T3 Negative Emotions ... .28** ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .57*** ... we regressed enacted incivility on predictors from this stage--experienced incivility (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40), negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.subcategory: relative-importance results likely misinterpreted
issues.description: The manuscript states that predictors accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility. Relative-importance metrics usually partition explained variance, not total outcome variance, and are highly sensitive when predictors are strongly intercorrelated. The manuscript does not specify the metric used or clarify whether these are percentages of R2, risking overinterpretation.
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.subcategory: work-hours control variable not described in measures
issues.description: Work hours appear in the correlation and regression tables and are included as controls, but the Measures section does not describe how work hours were assessed, at which waves, why T4 work hours were not used, or whether work hours were preregistered controls. Undescribed controls impede replication and interpretation.
issues.quote: T1 Work Hours | 36.29 | 9.83 ... T2 Work Hours | 37.54 | 8.26 ... T3 Work Hours | 37.13 | 7.93 ... T2 Work Hours ... T3 Work Hours

issues.subcategory: enacted incivility items may conflate clinical duties with rudeness
issues.description: Some adapted enacted-incivility items may not validly represent incivility in clinical care. For example, nurses may legitimately doubt a patient’s or family member’s judgment about medical matters or pay less attention to clinically irrelevant statements during high-acuity care. Without context, these items can conflate appropriate clinical boundary-setting or triage with uncivil behavior.
issues.quote: “Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility,” “Paid little attention to one or more patient’s/patient family members’ statements or showed little interest in their opinions,”

issues.subcategory: patient and family/friend incivility combined despite different constructs
issues.description: Experienced and enacted incivility combine patients with patient family members/friends, but the moderator is patient acuity and the theory often refers to patients. Family members may be uncivil for reasons unrelated to patient acuity, and nurses’ behavior toward family members differs from behavior toward patients. Combining these sources/targets obscures mechanisms and weakens construct alignment.
issues.quote: any of your patients or patient family members/friends ... The incivility examined is therefore incivility from patients and their families (experienced incivility) and incivility towards patients and their families (enacted incivility). ... what percentage of patients under your care in the past week would be considered "severe"?

issues.subcategory: compassion fatigue construct overlaps with proposed mediator and outcome
issues.description: Compassion fatigue is described as including irritability, aggression, cynicism, unresponsiveness, and indifference, which conceptually overlap with negative emotions and enacted incivility. This overlap creates criterion contamination in the mediation model: the mediator may partly measure affective hostility and uncivil tendencies rather than a distinct fatigue mechanism.
issues.quote: The burnout component of compassion fatigue relates to feelings of hopelessness, anxiety, irritability, aggression, cynicism, and difficulty in performing one’s job effectively or dealing with stressors from work ... outcomes – such as ... social (e.g., unresponsiveness or indifference towards customers)

issues.subcategory: compassion fatigue scale/timeframe not justified for weekly fluctuation
issues.description: Compassion fatigue is typically a cumulative burnout/secondary-trauma construct, but the study asks respondents to report it over the past week at each wave and treats week-to-week variation as a mediator. The manuscript does not establish that the Compassion Fatigue-Short Scale is valid for weekly state-like assessment or that its burnout and secondary-trauma components function similarly over such short intervals.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week. ... Compassion Fatigue. The Compassion Fatigue-Short Scale (Adams et al., 2006) asked participants, “Please indicate how often you experience the following at your job.”

issues.subcategory: negative-emotions scale may capture reactions to clinical risk rather than incivility
issues.description: The negative-emotions measure includes fear and disgust toward patients. In high-acuity clinical settings, fear may reflect safety risk or patient aggression, and disgust/aversion may reflect clinical exposure or burnout rather than emotional response to incivility. This weakens the specificity of the proposed mediator.
issues.quote: The scale items consisted of four negative emotions: (a) aversion, (b) disgust, (c) anger, (d) fear.

issues.subcategory: adapted shortened scales lack sufficient validation details
issues.description: The study shortens and adapts established scales, including changing 'customer' to 'patient' and selecting highest-loading items. Although pilot correlations are reported, the manuscript does not provide item loadings, factor correlations, full pilot psychometrics, measurement invariance across waves, or evidence that shortened adapted scales preserve content validity in clinical contexts.
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length ... the word “customer” was replaced with “patient” or “patient or patient family members/friends” ... assessed part-whole correlations between the full scales and shortened versions during pilot testing

issues.subcategory: no longitudinal measurement invariance testing
issues.description: Because the study relies on changes and lagged relations across four repeated waves, measurement invariance over time is important. The manuscript reports a CFA but does not report configural, metric, or scalar invariance across waves. Without invariance, apparent longitudinal relations could reflect changing measurement properties rather than construct stability or change.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks. ... Before evaluating our hypotheses, we investigated the discriminant validity of our measures by employing a series of confirmatory factor analyses.

issues.subcategory: no a priori power analysis for interaction and indirect effects
issues.description: The manuscript does not report an a priori power analysis. This is especially problematic for moderation, moderated mediation, and indirect effects, which require larger samples and were tested with only N = 244 after acuity missingness. Non-significant conditional indirect effects may reflect insufficient power rather than absence of moderation.
issues.quote: Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable. ... the slopes at low ... medium ... and high levels ... of perceived patient acuity were all non-significant.

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from specialized nursing sample to service employees/customers
issues.description: The sample consists of mostly female nurses in high-stakes healthcare settings, recruited nonprobabilistically. The manuscript nevertheless frames conclusions broadly in terms of service employees, customers, and service industries. Healthcare involves ethical duties, clinical authority constraints, illness-related patient behavior, and family involvement that differ from ordinary customer service.
issues.quote: Using a four-wave data collection of service employees within the healthcare industry ... Because incivility from customers is likely a common experience for employees in the service industries ... Our results suggest that experiencing incivility from customers can have negative downstream costs for how future customers are treated.

issues.subcategory: patient-nurse relationship treated as customer-employee relationship despite important differences
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that nurse-patient relationships are more complex than customer-employee relationships but continues to use customer-incivility theory and terminology. Patients may be ill, cognitively impaired, afraid, involuntarily present, dependent on care, and embedded in family/team care systems. These differences affect norms, intent, reciprocity, and interpretations of incivility, limiting theoretical equivalence.
issues.quote: We view the patient-nurse relationship as a specialized form of customer-employee relationship. However, it is important to understand that this relationship includes care provision and care coordination, which is more complex and dynamic than some other employee-customer relationships.

issues.subcategory: unmeasured clinical and organizational confounding
issues.description: Patient acuity, experienced incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility may all be driven by unmeasured factors such as unit type, staffing ratios, shift length, nurse-to-patient ratio, patient cognitive status, psychiatric/substance-use presentations, violence exposure, leadership climate, and baseline negative affectivity. The autoregressive design does not eliminate these time-varying confounds.
issues.quote: Within this study, we look at perceptions of patient acuity across all patients seen within a given work week as a potential stressor that may be exacerbating the negative effects of experienced incivility. ... nurses working with multiple patients simultaneously and transferring care to other nurses at the end of their shifts.

issues.subcategory: practice implication overstates unsupported moderated behavioral pathway
issues.description: The supplemental moderated mediation analyses found that the indirect effect on enacted incivility was not conditional on patient acuity. Yet the practice section claims that employees with high incivility and high acuity are at highest risk of fatigue and ultimately enacted incivility. This extrapolates beyond the supported moderation, which was only for the incivility-to-negative-emotions path.
issues.quote: the slopes at low ... medium ... and high levels ... of perceived patient acuity were all non-significant. ... Taken together, these results reveal the indirect effect is not conditional upon perceived patient acuity. ... employees experiencing incivility from patients and who have a high perceived patient acuity load are at the highest risk of experiencing increased negative affect and fatigue and, ultimately, engaging in incivility.

issues.subcategory: opaque high-volume data-quality exclusions
issues.description: Seventy-eight respondents were excluded for poor data quality, including 56 for not providing 'reasonably consistent' demographic responses. The thresholds for reasonable consistency are not specified, and no comparison of excluded versus retained respondents on focal variables is reported. Such large exclusions can materially affect results and require transparent, preregistered rules and sensitivity analyses.
issues.quote: Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics: (a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age); ... This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: survey administration and wave-linking details missing
issues.description: The manuscript does not explain how participants were recontacted for later waves, how responses were linked across waves, what reminders were used, how duplicate participation was prevented before analysis, or whether unique survey links were used. These details are essential for evaluating longitudinal online data quality.
issues.quote: Participants received a $5 gift card for each survey they completed ... no participant emails were obtained or used during the recruitment process ... participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys

issues.subcategory: ethics/IRB approval not reported
issues.description: The study involved working nurses reporting potentially sensitive information about mistreating patients and experiencing distress. The manuscript mentions consent information but does not report IRB/ethics approval, consent procedures, confidentiality safeguards beyond general assurance, or data-protection procedures.
issues.quote: highlighted the high stakes/critical care focus in the recruitment and consent information ... ensured respondents of the confidentiality of their results

issues.subcategory: tables are malformed and hard to audit
issues.description: The tables contain duplicated headers, repeated notes, missing/garbled entries, and an incomplete R2 entry. This makes it difficult to verify model specification and results. Poor table formatting is not merely cosmetic when central coefficients and sample sizes are already inconsistent.
issues.quote: Table 3 ... R2 | . |  |  | .24 ... Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.  * p < .05 ** p < .01 *** p < .001 | Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.subcategory: compassion fatigue mechanism insufficiently tied to incivility exposure
issues.description: Compassion fatigue is defined as arising from exposure to others’ suffering, high stress, and trauma, yet the model treats patient incivility as a key antecedent via negative emotions. Incivility and traumatic caregiving exposure are conceptually different stressors. Without measuring trauma exposure or caregiving intensity separately, the proposed compassion-fatigue mechanism may be theoretically underspecified.
issues.quote: Caregiving employees have a duty to routinely care for others, in turn exposing them to others’ suffering, high stress, and trauma ... We propose that negative emotions generated due to incivility experiences may be an important reason for why repeated exposure to customer incivility may place employees at increased risk of experiencing compassion fatigue.

issues.subcategory: variable work exposure during weekly recall not adequately controlled
issues.description: Nurses may work different numbers of shifts, 12-hour schedules, or compressed workweeks, producing different exposure opportunities for patient incivility and enacted incivility. Work hours appear as a control but are not described, and number of shifts, patient volume, unit type, and direct patient-contact hours are not measured or controlled. This threatens comparability of weekly frequency reports.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week. ... worked more than one shift a week, on average ... In combination with condensed 3-day work weeks

issues.subcategory: frequency scale lacks exposure denominator
issues.description: Experienced and enacted incivility are measured as frequency over the past week, but nurses differ in number of patients, family interactions, shifts, and hours worked. Without an exposure denominator, higher scores may reflect more patient contacts rather than greater incivility propensity or climate.
issues.quote: Thinking about your experiences at work during the past week, how often have you been in a situation where any of your patients or patient family members/friends... ... Thinking about your interactions with patients during the past week, how often have you...?

issues.subcategory: moderation probing incompletely specified
issues.description: The manuscript reports low, medium, and high levels of patient acuity but does not explicitly state in the Results whether these are mean and ±1 SD, whether values were within the observed range after centering, or whether Johnson-Neyman regions were examined. This matters because the moderator is bounded and highly missing.
issues.quote: Simple slope analysis estimates at low (B = .13, SE = .12, p = .26, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.35]), medium (B = .22, SE = .09, p < .05, 95% CI [0.04, 0.40]), and high (B = .32, SE = .08, p < .001, 95% CI [0.17, 0.46]) levels of the moderator

issues.subcategory: non-significant direct effect obscured by mediation language
issues.description: The final direct path from experienced incivility to enacted incivility in Table 2 is negative and non-significant, yet the discussion refers to a 'partial mediation process' for future incivility enactment. Partial mediation would require a remaining direct effect; otherwise the evidence supports only an indirect association under the specified model.
issues.quote: Our results support a partial mediation process: in support of our hypotheses, experiencing incivility from patients was related to increased future incivility enactment towards patients indirectly through increased negative emotions towards patients and compassion fatigue. ... T2 Customer Incivility ... Enacted Incivility (T4) ... -.07 | .05 | -1.14
